tickets.title: SELECT & WHERE
tickets.description: Writes a query to retrieve active customers from the USA who signed up after '2024-01-01'.
tasks: Writes a query to retrieve active customers from the USA who signed up after '2024-01-01'.
learning_objectives: Understand relational database design and querying.
tickets.evaluation: `compare_result_set(actual, expected)` `check_projected_fields(actual, included=['id', 'name', 'email', 'country', 'signed_up_at'], excluded=[])` `check_sort_order(actual, 'signed_up_at', 'DESC')` **[A] Correctness (40 pts)**: 40 pts if exact result set matches; 20 pts if USA filtered correctly but order is wrong. **[B] Optimality (30 pts)**: 30 pts if query executes in `< 5ms`; 10 pts if execution takes longer due to sub-optimal scans. **[C] Quality (20 pts)**: 20 pts if keywords are uppercase (`SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`); 10 pts if lowercase.
common_mistakes: Forgetting semicolons at the end of statements.
Using reserved keywords as column names without backticks.
hints: Review the MySQL documentation for exact syntax.
Test your queries in smaller chunks first.

solution.query.sql:
SELECT id, name, email, country, signed_up_at
    FROM customers
    WHERE country = 'USA' AND status = 'active' AND signed_up_at >= '2024-01-01'
    ORDER BY signed_up_at DESC;

tickets.title: Pattern Matching & Sorting
tickets.description: Writes a query to select all customers whose names start with 'A', sorted by signup date DESC.
tasks: Writes a query to select all customers whose names start with 'A', sorted by signup date DESC.
learning_objectives: Understand relational database design and querying.
tickets.evaluation: `compare_result_set(actual, expected)` `check_command_used("LIKE")` `check_sort_order(actual, 'signed_up_at', 'DESC')` **[A] Correctness (40 pts)**: 40 pts for correct name filters and sort; 0 pts if `LIKE` pattern is incorrect. **[B] Optimality (30 pts)**: 30 pts for direct scanning using index. **[C] Quality (20 pts)**: 20 pts for structured indentation and casing.
common_mistakes: Forgetting semicolons at the end of statements.
Using reserved keywords as column names without backticks.
hints: Review the MySQL documentation for exact syntax.
Test your queries in smaller chunks first.

solution.query.sql:
SELECT id, name, email, signed_up_at
    FROM customers
    WHERE name LIKE 'A%'
    ORDER BY signed_up_at DESC;

tickets.title: Monthly Sales Revenue (HAVING)
tickets.description: Calculates total sales revenue and average order value for each month in 2024. Filters out months with total sales less than or equal to $500.
tasks: Calculates total sales revenue and average order value for each month in 2024.
Filters out months with total sales less than or equal to $500.
learning_objectives: Understand relational database design and querying.
tickets.evaluation: `compare_result_set(actual, expected)` `check_command_used("GROUP BY")` `check_command_used("HAVING")` **[A] Correctness (40 pts)**: 40 pts if aggregate sales matches; 20 pts if grouped by month but HAVING clause is missing. **[B] Optimality (30 pts)**: 30 pts if status filter executes first (reducing scan size). **[C] Quality (20 pts)**: 20 pts for using `ROUND()` to format aggregate decimal fields.
common_mistakes: Forgetting semicolons at the end of statements.
Using reserved keywords as column names without backticks.
hints: Review the MySQL documentation for exact syntax.
Test your queries in smaller chunks first.

solution.query.sql:
SELECT
      DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
      SUM(total_amount) AS total_sales,
      ROUND(AVG(total_amount), 2) AS avg_order_value
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m')
    HAVING SUM(total_amount) > 500
    ORDER BY order_month ASC;
